messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: beta fails with [0, 1] data
parts:
This is a report on some behavior I found interesting, not a request for
help.

y is a variable ranging from 0 through 5 which I rescaled with
z <- (0.1 + y)/5.2;
to be inside (0, 1). Most of the values are at the extremes.

Treating z as drawn from a beta distribution, this fit fine.

Since the fit distribution was U-shaped, I figured there was no reason
to pull the range in, since it was allowed to have mass at the
extremes. This couldn't get off the ground:

Error in function stan::prob::beta_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Second shape parameter[0] is 0:0, but must be > 0!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
Initialization failed after 100 attempts. Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

Perhaps this has something to do with my parametrization in terms of the
mean.

For the curious, here's the model:

data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
int<lower=0> J; //number of covariates
int<lower=0> NSD; // number of classes of beta for sd
int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J]; // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
int<lower=0> NCLUSTER; //number of seeds
int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
matrix[N, J] x; // covariates
vector<lower=0,upper=5>[N] y; // outcome
}
transformed data {
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] z;
z <- y/5.0;
}
parameters {
vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
real<lower=0> nu; // 'size' parameter
real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;
real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
vector[J] beta;
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
for(ir in 1:J) {
beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
}
alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma_alpha;
}
model {
vector[N] mu;
vector[N] parm1;
vector[N] parm2;
nu ~ cauchy(0, 5); //maybe it should start above 0
sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 5);
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
for (j in 2:J) {
beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
}
alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
for (n in 1:N) {
mu[n] <- inv_logit((x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]]);
}
parm1 <- mu*nu;
parm2 <- (1-mu)*nu;
z ~ beta(parm1, parm2);

Ross Boylan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] beta fails with [0, 1] data
parts:
y ~ beta(a,b) isn't going to work with y == 0 or y == 1.
Just follow the definition of beta and you'll see it leads
to zero probability, because there are y^(a-1) and (1-y)^(b-1)
terms in the distribution.

I just added a to-do item for the manual to make that clear
in the doc for the distributions.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] beta fails with [0, 1] data
parts:
On Mar 10, 2014, at 6:27 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:

> On Sat, 2014-03-08 at 20:30 +0100, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> y ~ beta(a,b) isn't going to work with y == 0 or y == 1.
>> Just follow the definition of beta and you'll see it leads
>> to zero probability, because there are y^(a-1) and (1-y)^(b-1)
>> terms in the distribution.
> y^(a-1) -> infinity and y->0 if a<1

I don't follow. y is an argument to the function. If
y = 0, then y^(a-1) == 0. If y = 1, then (1-y)^(b-1) == 0.

As a -> 0 and b -> 0, then the probability mass concentrates
around either 0 or 1. I don't know if we set up the
function to return non-zero results for the
boundary conditions of (a = 0, b > 0, y = 0) or (a > 0, b = 0, y = 1).

Or maybe you're thinking about the log scale, because log(0) = -infinity?

- Bob

You don't need to be at the boundary to run into infinity. In fact,

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] beta fails with [0, 1] data
parts:
Right --- 0^x is non-zero by convention for convenience in
some places. In the C++ lib, it's unspecified behavior
that's implementation dependent:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/pow/

but is allowed to raise an error.

What Stan actually does for the probability functions is work
on the log scale, so it's

log(0^x) = x log(0) = x * -inf, which is either +/- inf

depending on the sign of x, and when converted back to the
linear scale is either 0 or inf, as you say.

We should definitely specify the behavior for beta(y|alpha,beta)
in these cases --- I don't think it makes sense to follow the
convention and have infinite density --- we should be raising an
exception.

- Bob
